chapter_theme: The first half of the plaint to the heart (நெஞ்சொடு புலம்பல்): Pattinathar tells his heart what it failed to do, praise the teacher who dances in the cremation ground, the Lord beyond the three voids, the true guru and the holy feet, and what it did instead, took gold, house, women, kin and the body as lasting, hoarded and buried wealth, and gave nothing to the hungry or the learned. Against each failure stands Yama, who takes the life while rings, retinue, kin and buried gold stay where they are.
structure_note: Four-line stanzas, nearly all closing on நெஞ்சமே (O heart) after a negative participle (போற்றாமல், ஈயாமல், not praising, not giving) and a verb of what the heart did. 641 addresses பாழ்மனமே instead; 648 and 661 end in the first person (ஆனேனே) and 657 and 659 drop the address. 647 alone is instruction rather than reproach: the poet tells the heart what to think.

637.reading: Not praising the teacher who dances in the red cremation ground, having shown earth, gold and the darkness of maya for what they are, you were caught in the eye-nets of women who flash their eyes and talk, and wandered like a dog in the market, O heart.
637.nuance: மண், பொன் and the women of line 3 are the three cravings of Tamil moral talk (land, gold, women). தேசிகன் is the teacher; the dancer of the red ground is Siva, so the guru and the Lord are one figure.

638.reading: Lying on a flower couch and a gold-silk mattress, in peerless ornaments and with your gold never out of reach, before Yama takes the life from this mat you lie on, you did not praise and embrace the Threefold Void, O heart.
638.nuance: முப்பாழ், the three voids, is used as a name of the Lord (also 639, 658), as in the Arutpulambal's close (618). The silk mattress becomes இப்பாய், this mat, in the line where Yama arrives.

639.reading: The three voids void, the first void bare void, and beyond that void he dances; not praising him, trusting this life that is itself a void, and giving nothing to those who came begging, you let yourself be ringed by the deeds that came as your strength, O heart.
639.nuance: The first two lines pile பாழ் six times: the three voids, the first void, the void beyond, and this life as a void. துப்பாழாய் is obscure; துப்பு ஆழாய் (as your deep strength) or a corrupt துர்ப்பாழ் are both possible. ஏற்றவர் are those who come to receive, beggars.

640.reading: Given a birth in which to share rice and help those who wander here, you did not praise Siva's grace, and thought gold, house, lovely women and this life were still permanent, O heart.
640.nuance: சதம், permanent, is the recurring error-word of the plaint (644, 657). The verse makes human birth an opportunity for giving before it is one for worship.

641.reading: Not thinking that the wealth that came by the order of what you did in earlier lives was got only today, waste heart, you gave nothing to the destitute, did not consider Hara's worship, gave nothing to the learned, and forgot it all.
641.nuance: முற்றொடர்பு, the earlier connection, is past births; wealth is the fruit of former deeds and so not one's own achievement. The two classes owed a share, அற்றவர் and கற்றவர், are the destitute and the learned.

642.reading: Though you wear ruby, pearl and diamond and sit on a throne of pure gold, when Yama marks the body and takes it by the hand, we do not see the pure gold come along, O heart.
642.nuance: காணிப்பொன் and ஆணிப்பொன் are both fine gold; the gold that measured status stays on the throne.

643.reading: Though you wear a jewelled ring, fine ear-studs and a waist-cord, and become one of the lords honoured in each of the eight directions, when Yama plays ball with the life, we do not see your retinue come along, O heart.
643.nuance: கைச்சட்டம் is obscure: a hand ornament matching the ring and studs, or a band of followers. பற்கிட்ட (teeth clenched) describes Yama at play. The verse repeats 642 with rank in place of wealth.

644.reading: Unless the austerity you did before gathers in as all three, will gold, jewels and women come to you there? Not holding the true guru as your lasting good, you have become sightless like a blind man, O heart.
644.nuance: முப்பாலும் may be the three goods (virtue, wealth, pleasure) that past tapas yields, or a third of the account; the line says only that gold and women are the fruit of past merit, not of this life's striving. அந்தகன் is both a blind man and Yama.

645.reading: Not plucking pure flowers to worship and bow at the golden feet of the Supreme who wears the hooded serpent, you were proud, taking the bangles on the hand and the anklets on the foot for the truth, O heart.
645.nuance: The bangles and anklets are women's; the heart's truth was the ornamented body of the beloved, against which the verse sets the simplest ritual act, a flower at the feet.

646.reading: Not striving even once a day to praise the golden feet of Hara who gave the Lady half of himself, you sought wealth for contention and buried it in this earth: where did you think you were going, O heart?
646.nuance: வாதுக்குத் தேடி, seeking in order to argue or compete, is acquisition as rivalry; burying it in the ground is the hoarder's habit the verse turns into a question about destination.

647.reading: Heart, I tell you a thought: praising the grace of the five, cut off the five senses; put away deceit, and so that no second thought comes, meditate on the red feet.
647.nuance: அஞ்சருள் is read as the grace of the five, the five letters (அஞ்செழுத்து, 659) or the five-faced Lord; it is set against the five senses in the same line. The one stanza of the plaint that instructs rather than reproaches.

648.reading: Before this strange body and breath subside, I did not praise the true guru and gain austerity to live by, but trusted new-made gold, possessions and a great life, and became like a frog in a serpent's mouth.
648.nuance: The frog in the snake's mouth is still alive and still trusting; the image is of a man already taken who does not know it.

649.reading: Who are kin, who are parents, who are brothers, who are children? Whoever is there, will they help when you die? Melting like a young calf that has lost its cow, you joined yourself to petty pleasures, O heart.
649.nuance: கற்றா is the milch-cow (கன்று + ஆ); the calf's melting for its mother is the heart's dependence on kin, which the questions have just emptied.

650.reading: The house still there, the mother there, the needed wife there, honour there, food there, the children there, the cattle and calf there, the saved wealth there, and the cage itself there, you went: what a state, what a state that was.
650.nuance: கூடு, the cage or nest, is the body, left behind with everything else; the one who went is the life. The list has nine things that stay and one that goes.

651.reading: Sandal, kumkum, paste and perfumes wondrously smeared, finery and swagger, and the girls who wear fragrant flowers all still here, you did not consider in what manner you went, O heart.
651.nuance: Continues 650: the second list of what stays is the apparatus of pleasure and the women who shared it.

652.reading: Proud that you have fed the leaking bag of wind, this body of filth given over to harsh deeds, you did not look with pity and give rice to the hungry, but spread yourself abroad like a river in flood, O heart.
652.nuance: காற்றுத் துருத்தி is the bellows or wind-bag; ஊற்றைச் சடலம் the oozing body. அளாவினை, you spread and mixed, is the heart's dissipation set against the one directed act of feeding.

653.reading: Trusting this bubble life as a certainty, not giving even a nut's worth of rice to the hungry, you did not consider who would stand by you when Yama's messenger seizes and drags you in that struggle, O heart.
653.nuance: பாக்களவாம் அன்னம், rice the size of an areca-nut, is the least possible gift. ஆர்ப் படுவார் is read as 'who will be bound (with you)', that is, who will share it.

654.reading: Through the many wiles of a woman with a small brow, the breasts budding and swelling on her chest and their colour glistening, you were dazed and caught in the net, and never learned to share rice and eat, O heart.
654.nuance: சிலந்தி is a spider and also a kind of boil or swelling; here 'what sprouted on her chest and swelled' is read as the breasts. சின்னஞ்சிறு நுதலாள், she of the small brow, is a conventional beauty.

655.reading: Not praising with all your might the grace of the Siva-siddha who works this holed bag, this perishing worm-nest, you did not consider that the thing he shows is this: to open the house and summon the open space by light, O heart.
655.nuance: The third line is cipher: வீடு is the house (body) and release, வெளி the open space (the inner sky), ஒளி the light; tradition takes it as the yogic opening of the body's door so that the inner space is seen by light. The Lord is called சிவசித்தர், the siddha who moves the body as a puppet.

656.reading: Beyond carrying this flesh-packed body, this worm-nest, you did nothing, not praising the true guru; and seeing the forest-wide flood break its banks and go, you scattered into worry like fish spreading in it, O heart.
656.nuance: The fish spreading as the flood breaks is the mind dispersing with events; விசாரம் is anxiety, not inquiry.

657.reading: Taking as permanent the frame in which the life is shut up, and leaning on it in pride, when Yama breaks that frame and takes the life, the wealth you kept hidden will not come there.
657.nuance: உடக்கை is read as the body (உடல்) or its covering; சடக்கு the frame. The hidden wealth (அடக்கமாய் வைத்த பொருள்) picks up the buried gold of 646.

658.reading: Not praising the Threefold Void, the sweet honey, the clear nectar that never cloys, the seed of release, you let yourself be ringed by deeds that stand round you so that Yama grips you and binds you with his noose, O heart.
658.nuance: The void is given the sweetest names: honey, nectar, seed of release. முத்திக்கு வித்து makes the Lord the cause of release, and deeds (வினை) the ring that Yama's noose closes.

659.reading: Not praising the Lord who stands as the five letters, the eight letters, the fifty-one letters and the tender letter, caught in the net of deceitful full-breasted women, we chattered and searched and poured water on waste ground.
659.nuance: The counts are the mantra-letters of Saiva practice: five (நமசிவாய), eight, and the fifty-one letters of the alphabet; பிஞ்செழுத்து, the unripe or tender letter, is the Siddhars' name for the one subtle letter behind them, as in Sivavakkiyar. பாழுக்கு இறைத்தல், watering waste ground, is labour lost. பஞ்சரித்து is read as chattering.

660.reading: Not worshipping the holy feet of Sokkar who wears bone, arugu grass, konrai, thumbai and the crescent moon, you trusted the life with children, wives and kin and lovingly thought it would be there for all time, O heart.
660.nuance: சொக்கர் is Siva of Madurai; அக்கு is bone, worn as beads. எக்காலமும் உண்டு, 'exists for all time', is the heart's creed against which the plaint is written.

661.reading: Not greatly praising the grace of the guru who took me, not looking for the way to the house of Kailasa, I fell into the false maya of women with braided hair and became a kendai fish writhing on the hook.
661.nuance: கயிலாய வீடு, the house of Kailasa, is release named as a place; ஆண்ட குரு is the guru who ruled or claimed him. The hooked fish of this verse becomes the poisoned fish of 668.

links.note: Both stanzas place the Lord beyond the three voids as முதற்பாழ், the first void: in the Arutpulambal he comes and swallows the soul, in the plaint he dances there unpraised while the heart trusts a life that is itself a void.

The Kural says wealth does not stay, so do at once what stays; Pattinathar's heart, given a birth in which to share rice, thought gold, house and women permanent instead. Both make giving the lasting use of a passing thing.

The Naladiyar says share the food of blameless wealth from the day it comes, because it turns like a cart wheel; Pattinathar adds that it came by earlier deeds and was not got today, and that the destitute and the learned were owed a share.

Tirumular's dying man leaves while the kohl-eyed wife and the wealth stay behind; Pattinathar's jewelled lord on a golden throne does not see the gold come along when Yama takes his hand. Same scene from the same side.

The Naladiyar says those who live on earlier austerity and do none now will stand outside the house grieving; Pattinathar says gold and women come only from austerity done before, and the heart that does not hold to the guru now is blind. Both treat present fortune as spent merit.

Arunagirinathar asks to join the devotees before his body falls into Death's tongue like a frog into a snake's mouth; Pattinathar says he has already become the frog in the serpent's mouth, trusting gold. One prays before the image, the other confesses from inside it.

Sivavakkiyar asks whether children, wives and kin can come along when Death calls; Pattinathar asks who among kin, parents, brothers and children will help when one dies. The same rhetorical question put to the heart.

The Kural pictures the body and life parting as a bird flying off and leaving its nest alone; Pattinathar ends his list of everything that stays with கூடு, the cage or nest, left while 'you' went. The nest is the body in both.

Arunagirinathar names the body a leaking bag of wind among his string of bags; Pattinathar calls it the wind-bellows and the oozing corpse. Arunagirinathar asks to be rid of it, Pattinathar faults the heart for feeding it instead of the hungry.

The Naladiyar says give at once what comes to hand, for those who gave first escape the waste land through which Death drags his captives; Pattinathar's heart gave not a nut's worth of rice and did not ask who would stand by it when Yama's messenger drags it. Giving is the only provision for that journey in both.
The Naladiyar's firm see the body as a bubble in pelting rain; Pattinathar's heart trusted the water-bubble life as certain. Same image, opposite minds.

Tirumular says that if one door is closed inside the bag, light shines in the body and the black-daubed temple is lit with a gem lamp; Pattinathar's Siva-siddha shows how to open the house and summon the open space by light in the holed bag. Both make the body a bag with a door and light the thing to be found in it, though one closes the door and the other opens it.

Tirumular makes the Lord's feet the eight letters and his anklets twice five and fifty-one; Pattinathar's Lord stands as five letters, eight letters and fifty-one. The same letter-counts name the same Lord, and in both the counting ends in a single subtle thing (the tender letter, the feet).

Sivavakkiyar demands the straight truth of the unripe letter (பிஞ்செழுத்து) that stands first among the five; Pattinathar's Lord stands as the tender letter behind the five, eight and fifty-one. The same cipher-word for the one letter behind the counted ones.

Sivavakkiyar's householder rejoices beside his mansions with cattle, wealth, wife and children when Death's messengers strike all at once; Pattinathar's heart trusted children, wives and kin and thought it would last for all time.

The Kural says the gambler's winnings are like the hook swallowed by a fish; Pattinathar is the kendai fish writhing on the hook of women's maya. The same hook, baited with winnings in one and with women in the other.

source_issues: 639 line 4 துப்பாழாய் is not a known word; the line may be corrupt.
643 line 4 கைச்சட்டம் is obscure and may be a misprint.
647 line 1 துற்க்க (for துறக்க) has a doubled consonant sign.
648 and 661 end in the first person (ஆனேனே) and 657 and 659 lack the address நெஞ்சமே that the other stanzas carry; 659 ends in the plural இறைத்தோமே.
